story_text.value:
Hi everyone. I’m a 19yo solo developer and I’m making a project called Phoam.

In middle school, I made a little games website for the people in my school, but it became surprisingly popular. Students would ask me to add mobile apps, and I remember searching how to run APKs online and not finding what I wanted.

I’ve always liked the idea that if software ran on one machine at some point, it should also run on another.

Apple dropped support for 32-bit apps many years ago, leaving tons of nostalgic games unplayable on modern iPhones. Some newer Android phones also no longer support 32-bit apps, meaning having an APK for an app is not enough to play it again.

I knew about projects like Wine and Ruffle that had made software run in a way it was never designed to, and one day I just decided to start my own engine!

Phoam runs supported Android APKs and early iOS IPAs in the browser. The apps’ original code runs locally on your device, so it isn’t streaming from another phone or computer. On an iPhone, you can add them to your home screen.

It’s still very early, and compatibility varies. The public demos are Replica Island and Explora-Ball, which I can legally share. You can try them at https://phoam.app/demos without an account. Uploading your own apps isn’t public yet, and using your own files would require the necessary rights.

Also worth saying, AI has helped a lot with the coding, but I’ve been directing the project and testing the results.

Which old Android or iOS game would you most want to play again?

title.value: Show HN: Android and iOS games running offline in the browser

story_text.value:
Inspired by this great talk by Hamish Todd about Conformal Geometric Algebra [1] I felt the urge to play with those conformal transformations myself and to learn more about geometric algebra.

In the original talk Hamish shows many interactive visualizations to make a point about properties of conformal transformations and their representation via Geometric Algebra.

My goal was to reverse engineer these visualizations just from the snippets shown in the talk.

I find the result very satisfying to play around with. [2] As educational tool it provides some good intuition for conformal transformations and their composition. I hope some of you might enjoy it as well, especially after watching the original talk by Hamish Todd.

On the technical side it is built on Threlte (Svelte+ThreeJS) and mostly handwritten with AI only being used for trying and debugging some shader code performance optimizations.

1: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q3as9SGmDdw 2: https://static.laszlokorte.de/conformal-3d/

story_text.value:
Hotel for one night in Livonia, Michigan, and the three lines: room $54.53, platform fee $0.50, Kinsona fee $1.36. $1.86 is all Kinsona earns. This was a live test booking that got cancelled to ensure booking plumbing is working and refunds hit credit card. Still waiting for my first $1.86 as we refund everything within free cancellation window. My background is in healthcare pricing and it has taught me a lot about prices no one can see.

I created Kinsona (https://kinsona.com/) with an idea of showing hotel guests what the room costs, inclusive of taxes and payment processing, and Kinsona fees as itemized. Essentially, Cost-Plus model, where we charge a transparent fee at checkout. We do not know of any booking site that shows its cut. No packages to sell. Just hotels.

I built it all alone (TanStack, Stripe) and I want to put this forward to see if this community can provide honest feedback on the experience and the idea.

I will appreciate if you can search your favorite hotel and compare the results with where you book your hotels today and tear down our pricing and interface. Would love your feedback on transparent Cost-Plus receipt.

Thanks All.

title.value: Show HN: Kinsona – a hotel booking site that shows its cut on every booking

story_text.value:
Hi Everyone, I'm Samyeer, I wrote KeyPad a while back; it’s still going strong.

Apple's Universal Control lets you use your Mac's keyboard and mouse with an iPad, but it doesn't support the iPhone…or anything else.

KeyPad lets you use your Mac Keyboard and Trackpad as a bluetooth keyboard and mouse for the iPhone, android phones, Tablets, TVs, Raspberry Pi and I just verified it on the iPhone Duo. You can:

Type on your iPhone using the Mac’s full Keyboard. Control the iPhone using your Mac’s mouse or trackpad. Switch between multiple paired devices at will. Supports Gaming controls, hold up to 6 keys down at a time. Test iOS app keyboard support without getting a dedicated bluetooth keyboard.

Some technical items:

Mouse control needs you to enable Assistive Touch on the iPhone. KeyPad uses bluetooth only, so does not need an apple account or a network connection. The app itself is less than 3MB, no external libraries.

KeyPad reached #11 in the US Mac App Store - Developer Tools category. Highest it has ever been.

Do try it out, let me know what you think.

https://bluetooth-keyboard.com

https://apps.apple.com/app/keypad-bluetooth-keyboard/id14916...

story_text.value:
Hello there

I built a little Chrome extension that analyzes the content elements on a page, scores their "usefulness" and labels them based on that score. What counts as useful can be customized to your preferences and interests, and it learns from your feedback on the scores.

Each element gets a badge with its score; hover it for more details.

I'm using Jev, so the basic analysis is very fast and very cheap. You need to add your Jev key and run the small local bridge (it's in the repo).

For deeper analysis (e.g. a pareto summary) you bring your preferred AI key.

Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/emjbfdcigbfojhdipap...

story_text.value:
Hi Hackernews, This is my go at an important issue which is making sure agents stick to their rules and context. After using agents and learning from the community on reddit, I decided to have a go at some of the most important problems surrounding how agents are built and deployed in production.

This is meant to be a control layer for agents. It gives the agent an identity, policy, and a vault that holds the important sensitive keys used in monetary and high consequential actions. While also allows developers and business owners to query the agents to know what happened, which agent did what, and what business value did it bring to the table.

Another important feature is that developers or managers of their agents can undo actions that were gotten wrong my their agents such as deleting tables in a db or a transaction.

Their is alot of goodies, dig deep and let me know what you think.

fyi, the project seems to have gone far already. Its not a funded project yet parading as a tool. This was due to my obsession with perfection. Even my tools tend to look like finished products. We live in a capitalist society by the way. Have a swing guys!!

title.value: Show HN: I built a tool that babysits your agents

story_text.value:
Ported to TypeScript from Motorola 68k assembly!

All the rats' behaviors are true to spec: Their distractions (sniffing, turning around, grooming, stopping) are all frame accurate and occur in the same ratios as the original. The artwork and animation speeds were extracted from the old bitmaps and jump instructions and are (as close as I can get) to being frame accurate.

Enhancements:

I ran tens of thousands of simulations and fixed a few unfair advantages rats had if they were in the outside lane—they would lurch forward quickly around the turns resulting in a 43% win rate as opposed to the 33% random roll rate one would expect. Now it's within 0.5% for every training level and every lane.

I also bumped the max rat count up to 8 possible rats, and added a "lane passing" animation. It looks hilarious to see two rats side by side in the same lane, gunning their way to the finish line. Gotta have fair rat races.

I also added my own names for the rats, inspired by Berkeley Systems' naming scheme.

Now we can all scream at our monitors urging Flamin' Furball to turn around and start waddling again like it's 1994.

Github: https://github.com/heyitsjames/rat-race

story_text.value:
My oldest two kids are off to college and since leaving we've been playing the Wordle and 'sharing' our solutions with each other. It's been a fun way to stay connected with them, and it's become a bit of a challenge to see if we can beat each other's solutions. This got me thinking about other ways I could connect with them. The thing about the Wordle is that it doesn't take a large commitment of time, you can just pull it out when you've a few spare minutes. So I set out to build a game that would borrow from many of the themes that keep pulling us back to Wordle. What I created is called Tōtle which fits another one of our (okay my) favorite things; Dad jokes and puns (as it’s pronounced total).

Here's how it works. You get five different numbers from a number pool 1 to 20, and a target from the remaining pool. Combine two at a time with + − × ÷, using all five numbers, every result a positive whole number, each puzzle always takes 4 moves. You get 3 rounds and 4 undos per round; a medal for fewest moves (perfect 4 = crown). There's a spoiler-free share card, like Wordle’s grid.

The combinatorics math works out like this: C(20,5) (that's choose 5 from 20) × 15 possible target numbers = 232,560 possible puzzles. An interesting side quest: exhaustive search discovered that exactly 6 can’t be solved. They all are from the group of 6 numbers: 3, 7, 16, 17, 19, 20. If any one of those is chosen as the target the other 5 cannot make the target. I'm not sure if there are any interesting reasons or patterns.

Every puzzle was sorted into 7 difficulty bands, by how many solutions each has, to provide a way to add increasing difficulty along the week. Sunday draws from the easiest 30%, Saturday from the hardest 3%, the game shows “harder than X% of puzzles” on the hardest days; Saturdays so far have been in the 98th–99th percentile of difficulty. 5 Saturdays were discovered to have exactly one answer (answer here means ways that only regroup or reorder the same moves count as one); the first is #68, Saturday, December 19, 2026.

A few things I'd love to know from y'all:

Difficulty: does the Sunday-to-Saturday curve feel right, and are Saturdays too hard? I've experimented with a mode that offers some help. But it's still under development.

First-time play: was anything confusing, like dragging vs. tapping or how rounds work?

Phones: How does it play on your phone vs your computer?

title.value: Show HN: Totle, daily math puzzle game; Saturday puzzles have the fewest answers

story_text.value:
I made an agent-native 3d/vfx engine.

Agents are good at making interesting scenes in Blender/Unreal/Nuke/etc. But these tools are fundamentally limited compared to what coding agents are capable of. Many simplifying assumptions are baked into these tools in order to fit human authoring methods.

In vork, agents write the whole scene as code, including their own shaders, materials, cameras and physics, and vork renders it on the GPU. The core API fits in about 2,500 tokens.

So, for example, almost every 3d engine assumes light moves in a straight line. Light near a black hole does not; so the best you can do in e.g. Blender is faking gravitational lensing. In vork, you can model it for real.

If you want a camera lens that simulates a dragonfly's eye, or realistically-modeled Fata Morgana, this is also possible in vork.

title.value: Show HN: Vork – headless 3D and VFX engine for agents
